summary:
We built Project ODYSSEUS, a health-monitoring system for astronauts on long missions. It has two parts:

The app. A guided daily health check with ORBI, an AI companion that runs entirely on the device. Part 1 checks the mind and mood: a face scan, a voice conversation with ORBI, inkblot and memory exercises, a colour test and a NASA-style reaction test. Part 2 checks the body: heart and vitals, grip and calf strength, and radiation and bone.
The hardware. A portable briefcase designed in Autodesk Fusion, with medical-grade sensors and four custom circuit boards built around a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5.
At the end of each check, ORBI writes the astronaut a personal letter and a "prescription" of small actions. The medical team gets a separate, detailed findings section.

Why it matters. On long missions, crews face isolation, fatigue, muscle and bone loss, and radiation, often far from Earth with delayed communication. ODYSSEUS makes daily monitoring quick and humane. It catches gradual changes early by comparing each person with their own baseline. It also gives the astronaut someone to talk to, so no one has to face the longest expedition alone.
details:
What it does. An 11-step guided check (about 10 minutes, and any step can be skipped):

Face check: the camera measures blinking, eye closure (PERCLOS), gaze and tension, then gives a personal reading.

Talk with ORBI: a free voice conversation. ORBI understands messy or emotional speech, reads emotion from both the words and how they are spoken (pace, loudness, hesitation), answers any question and saves the transcript.

Mind exercises: 2 random Rorschach inkblots out of 10 (ORBI reacts to each answer) and 2 random memory and reasoning questions out of a bank of 20, based on psychology research.

Color test: a 5-colour Stroop test that measures cognitive interference.

Reaction test: based on NASA's psychomotor vigilance test (PVT).

Heart & vitals: ECG, pulse wave, heart rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure and heart-rate variability.

Grip strength.

Leg (calf) strength.

Radiation & bone: live NOAA and NASA space-weather data, the ISS position, a dose model and a bone-loss estimate.

Analysis: a rule engine compares every result with the person's own baseline, needs a change on two sessions before raising an alert, and sorts findings into stable, attention, review or emergency.

Personal report: ORBI's letter, the prescription, quotes from the session and a section for the medical team.

An SOS screen is available at all times. It offers the Crew Medical Officer and private lines to the flight surgeon or psychologist (simulated in the prototype). Trend charts show each person's history over the mission.

How it works.

App: a web app (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) served by a small Python server that also runs the live data pipeline. The pipeline fetches, validates, caches and models the space-weather data, and keeps working offline from its cache.

On-device AI: ORBI runs in the browser on the laptop's graphics card using WebLLM with Llama 3.2. A small sentence-embedding model (MiniLM) understands answers by meaning. MediaPipe Face Landmarker handles the face scan, and the Web Speech API handles voice in and out.

Privacy: health data stays on the device.

Honesty: physical sensor readings are simulated in this prototype and always labelled "Simulated data". The app never gives a diagnosis.

Hardware design (theoretical, not built).

Briefcase: a production-intent design made with a parametric Fusion script. It has drafted 2.5 mm shells, a tongue-and-groove seam, bosses with heat-set inserts, a battery door, a connector panel and a lid with a 10.1" touchscreen.

Lid sensors: a near-infrared face camera with infrared lights, an infrared thermometer, microphones and a speaker.

Instruments: ECG, SpO2, blood pressure, a grip dynamometer, a leg-strength foot plate, an ultrasound probe, a temperature probe and a Timepix3 radiation detector.

Boards: four boards. The main computer uses a Raspberry Pi CM5, the medical acquisition board uses TI ADS1298R and ADS1262 with an isolation barrier, plus a power board and a lid interface board.

Goals. Detect deconditioning, fatigue and psychological strain early. Make daily checks something astronauts want to do. Give flight surgeons clear, trustworthy, baseline-based data.

Tools and languages. JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Python, WebLLM (Llama 3.2), transformers.js (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), MediaPipe, Web Speech API, Autodesk Fusion (Python API), Chrome, and ffmpeg for the demo film.
